strengths: Elegant theoretical foundation: The paper introduces an exact factorization of the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) into localized components via Cauchy matrices using rank-one updates.
Computational efficiency: The proposed L2G-Net bypasses the expensive $O(n^3)$ eigendecomposition required by classical spectral GNNs, achieving a quadratic $O(kn^2)$ complexity.

principled approximation: The inclusion of interface spectral sparsification provides a robust, theoretically-grounded way to control complexity and trade-off representation fidelity for arbitrary graph structures.

Strong empirical performance: On several heterophilous graph benchmarks, L2G-Net achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art architectures (such as Polynormer) while requiring orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters.
Improved interpretability: Through Grad-CAM analysis, the authors demonstrate that L2G-Net maintains a clear local inductive bias compared to global GFT and attention-based methods.
weaknesses: Scalability on non-modular graphs: For highly dense graphs or graphs without a natural community/modular structure, the interface size $k$ can be large, necessitating aggressive sparsification (up to 99.5%). The paper would benefit from a more detailed discussion on the performance degradation boundaries under such extreme sparsification.

Preprocessing overhead: Although bisection and sparsification are fast, building the hierarchical graph family (HGF) structure still introduces non-trivial preprocessing overhead on very large graphs, which might limit its applicability compared to purely local message-passing schemes.
Clarity on parameter sharing: Some architectural details in Section 5 regarding how local filters ($g_{r,p}$) are parameterized and shared across levels could be described with more clarity.

strengths: Strong Theoretical Foundation: The mathematical derivation of the exact GFT factorization using Cauchy factors for arbitrary partitions is highly elegant and rigorous, resolving eigenvalue degeneracies via deflation and establishing solid complexity bounds.

Computational Complexity Reduction: By avoiding full eigendecomposition, L2G-Net successfully reduces the computational complexity of the GFT from cubic $O(n^3)$ to quadratic $O(kn^2)$, making exact global-local spectral processing feasible for mid-sized graphs.

Excellent Parameter Efficiency: The empirical evaluation on heterophily benchmarks shows that L2G-Net achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results while using orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters compared to transformer-based approaches (such as Polynormer).

Enhanced Interpretability: The local-to-global design provides a natural locality bias that translates to highly localized node attribution (shown via Grad-CAM), which is more interpretable than global GFT or fully-attentive models.
weaknesses: Practical Hierarchy Depth in Experiments: While the theoretical framework supports arbitrary hierarchical levels ($L$), the real-world experiments (Section 6.2 and Table 3) appear to restrict the hierarchy to only 1 level (partitioning the graph into just two subgraphs). It is unclear how performance, runtime, and stability behave when using deeper hierarchies ($L > 1$) on these benchmarks.

Impact of Aggressive Sparsification: For several datasets, the sparsification ratio is extremely aggressive (e.g., preserving only 0.5% of interface edges). Although Theorem 4.1 provides bounds on the quadratic form, the paper lacks a detailed empirical analysis of how different levels of sparsification impact the GFT approximation error and subsequent GNN performance.

Scalability Limitations: Although $O(kn^2)$ is a major improvement over $O(n^3)$, quadratic complexity still poses a bottleneck for truly large-scale graphs (e.g., millions of nodes), meaning the approach is still primarily limited to mid-sized graphs.

strengths: Elegant and highly original theoretical framework that factorizes the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) into localized subgraph transforms connected via Cauchy matrices.
Addresses a fundamental limitation of spectral GNNs (the $O(n^3)$ complexity of global GFT) by reducing it to $O(kn^2)$ through hierarchical divide-and-conquer processing.
Includes a robust mechanism (interface sparsification with spectral guarantees) to handle graphs without natural hierarchical structures.
Strong empirical results on heterophily/long-range benchmarks, achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art transformer-based models while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters.
Excellent presentation, clear figures (especially Figure 1), and mathematically rigorous proofs provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The computational complexity of the factorization is still quadratic in the number of nodes ($O(kn^2)$), which limits scalability to extremely large graphs (e.g., millions of nodes) where linear-time methods ($O(|E|)$) like ChebNet or standard MPNNs are preferred.

In the real-world experiments (Section 6.2), the model only uses one level of hierarchy ($L=1$). This raises questions about the practical utility and performance of deeper hierarchical merges ($L > 1$) on real-world datasets.

The paper lacks a detailed training/inference wall-clock time comparison per epoch against popular polynomial spectral GNNs (e.g., ChebNet, BernNet) on GPUs, which is crucial for evaluating actual deep learning practitioner overhead.
The scale of the evaluated real-world graphs is relatively modest (up to ~24k nodes). Demonstration on larger benchmark datasets (e.g., from OGB) would strengthen the scalability claims.

strengths: Strong Theoretical Foundation: The paper successfully generalizes the rank-one update-based Cauchy factorization of the GFT from simple paths to arbitrary graphs and symmetric matrices. It rigorously addresses crucial edge cases such as repeated eigenvalues and zero perturbation projections using a deflation framework.

Innovative Local-to-Global Bridge: By inserting learnable spectral filters between the hierarchical levels of Cauchy factors, L2G-Net elegantly bridges the gap between purely local spatial message-passing and purely global spectral filtering. Theorem 5.1 formally proves that the expressiveness of L2G-Net strictly contains global spectral filters.

Overcoming the O(n^3) Bottleneck: The reduction of GFT computation complexity from cubic to quadratic (scaled by cut size k) is a significant contribution. The inclusion of localized interface sparsification with spectral guarantees (Theorem 4.1) ensures scalability to very large graphs (e.g., City-Networks with >500k nodes) where global GFT is intractable.

Impressive Empirical and Parameter Efficiency: The model performs competitively with state-of-the-art architectures (like graph transformers and space-state models) across diverse datasets (heterophily, long-range, transductive/inductive) while using orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters.
weaknesses: Quadratic Scalability Bottleneck: Although O(kn^2) is a substantial improvement over O(n^3), quadratic complexity in the number of nodes still limits applicability to extremely large web-scale graphs where linear-time O(|E|) message-passing algorithms are mandatory. The per-epoch training times in Table 11 clearly reflect this quadratic scaling behavior.

Sensitivity to Partitioning and Sparsification: The efficiency and accuracy of the method are heavily tied to the graph's hierarchical structure and the quality of the partition. For dense graphs without clear community structures, the model must rely on aggressive sparsification, which might discard critical topological information. An ablation study evaluating downstream accuracy as a function of the sparsification ratio (or edge retention fraction) is missing.

Complexity of the Architectural Description: The transition from the Cauchy factorization of the basis to the learnable filter stack (Equations 9 and 10) is dense and could benefit from a more intuitive step-by-step description or pseudocode of the forward pass in the main text to improve accessibility.

strengths: Innovative and theoretically-grounded exact factorization of the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) into subgraph GFTs combined via orthogonal Cauchy-like matrices (OCLM).

Solid complexity analysis and a practical greedy partitioning scheme combined with spectral sparsification that scales exact spectral processing to graphs with hundreds of thousands of nodes (e.g., London with 569k nodes).
Excellent expressiveness analysis proving that L2G-Net strictly contains the class of global spectral filters while preserving local inductive biases.

Extensive and high-quality empirical evaluations across diverse datasets (heterophilous, long-range, transductive, and inductive), demonstrating superior parameter efficiency and highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art Graph Transformers.
weaknesses: Although Cauchy factorization reduces GFT complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(kn^2)$, the $O(n^2)$ scaling of the forward pass is still super-linear and slower per-epoch than linear $O(|E|)$ message passing networks (as shown in Table 11).

The sensitivity of downstream task performance to the level of sparsification is not fully explored. On dense graphs like Tolokers, aggressive sparsification is needed, which could potentially discard structurally important spectral information.

The choice of hierarchy depth ($L=1$ for several datasets in Section 6.2) suggests that the hierarchical benefits are not fully exploited on those benchmarks. An ablation study on the hierarchy depth $L$ and its trade-off with accuracy and computation time would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Elegant and rigorous theoretical framework that generalizes the GFT factorization via Cauchy matrices to arbitrary symmetric matrices, providing a mathematically sound solution to the GFT scalability issue.

The proposed L2G-Net combines the expressive power of global spectral filters with the inductive bias of local spectral processing by inserting learnable filters inside the hierarchical Cauchy factorization steps.

Significant computational and memory complexity reduction from $O(n^3)$ to $O(kn^2)$ (and $O(n^2)$ under parallelized solvers), which makes exact spectral processing feasible on large-scale graphs (e.g., City-Networks with >500k nodes) that were previously completely out of reach.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations spanning synthetic scaling analyses, transductive heterophily tasks, long-range inductive benchmarks, and large-scale transductive datasets. The results demonstrate competitive performance with drastically fewer parameters compared to state-of-the-art spatial/attention-based models.
Excellent qualitative analysis, including the visualization of learned local/global filters, Grad-CAM attribution studies showing localization properties, and thorough memory usage profiling.
weaknesses: While $O(kn^2)$ is a substantial improvement over $O(n^3)$, the quadratic complexity in terms of the number of nodes $n$ still limits the scalability of L2G-Net on truly web-scale graphs (e.g., millions of nodes) compared to $O(|E|)$ linear-time message-passing methods.

The method's efficiency is highly dependent on the graph possessing a hierarchical structure with small cuts. For dense or expander-like graphs, L2G-Net must rely on aggressive spectral sparsification, which might discard critical topological information for specific downstream tasks.

The preprocessing phase requires selecting non-trivial hyperparameters, such as the decomposition levels $L$ and sparsification ratio, which increases the engineering effort compared to simple spectral baselines.
